extracted.intended_audience: filmmakers, television producers, film/TV students, and general readers interested in production techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for choosing and using a single-camera vs. multi-camera setup in film and television production, including typical use-cases, trade-offs, and practical techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-camera setup (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this setup, all of the various shots and camera angles are taken using the same camera, or multiple cameras pointed in one direction, which are moved and reset to get a new angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also known as portable single crew/portable single camera or single-cam; developed during Classical Hollywood cinema and remains standard for cinema. Emphasizes that shots/angles are captured sequentially (or with moved/reset cameras) rather than simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-production editing flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Choices can then be made during the post-production editing process for when in the scene to use each shot, and when to cut back and forth between the two (or usually more than two) angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because each angle is shot separately (often with relighting and re-running the scene), editors can remove parts of a scene if it is too long and select exact cut points; director shoots actor A then B, relights, and runs the scene from each angle to enable editorial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple cameras for different framings in single-camera production
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, sometimes two cameras shooting from the same angle are used: one to capture a medium shot, the other a close-up during the same take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hybrid practical note: even within a single-camera-mode production, multiple cameras may be deployed for efficiency while preserving single-camera-style control over other setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-camera setup (definition and lighting constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multiple-camera setup consists of multiple cameras arranged to capture all of the different camera angles of the scene simultaneously, and the set must be lit to accommodate all camera setups concurrently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because cameras capture simultaneously, lighting must be a compromise that works for all planned angles; this imposes technical and aesthetic constraints relative to single-camera lighting per-shot control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed-versus-versatility trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-camera production generally results in faster but less versatile videography, whereas the single-camera setup is more time-consuming but gives the director more control over each shot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multi-camera when speed and efficiency are priorities; use single-camera when shot-by-shot control, bespoke lighting, and varied camera movement are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television producers must choose camera mode deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike film producers, who almost always opt for single-camera shooting, television producers need to make a distinct decision to shoot in either single-camera or multiple-camera mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames the production decision as deliberate and context-dependent rather than default; choices affect schedule, budget, style, and technical workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres typically suited to single-camera
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-camera is mostly reserved for prime time dramas, made-for-TV movies, music videos and commercial advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These genres favor cinematic visuals, controlled lighting and camera movement; single-camera supports film-like visual style and extensive post-production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres typically suited to multi-camera
rubrics_metrics.description: Soap operas, talk shows, game shows, reality television series, and sitcoms usually use the multiple-camera setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These genres often require efficiency, continuous performance capture, or live/studio conditions where simultaneous coverage is advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to record live-audience ensemble performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple-camera shooting is the only way that an ensemble of actors presenting a single performance before a live audience can be recorded from multiple perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If capturing a live, staged performance from multiple viewpoints in real time (e.g., taped before a studio audience) is required, multi-camera is effectively mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost/time considerations favor multi-camera for domestic sitcoms
rubrics_metrics.description: For standard, dialogue-driven domestic situation comedies, the multi-camera technique, which is cheaper and takes less production time, is typically used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When budget and rapid episode turnaround are priorities for conventional sitcom formats, multi-camera is the pragmatic choice despite aesthetic trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer single-camera for feature film-like visual style and frequent visual effects
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be deemed preferable to use the single-camera technique especially if specific camera angles and camera movements for a feature film-like visual style are considered crucial to the success of the production, and if visual effects are to be frequently used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-camera allows custom lighting and camera movement per shot and supports VFX workflows (e.g., multiple takes, compositing) that are difficult with multi-camera; choose it when stylistic and effects demands outweigh cost/time concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-camera supports tightly edited action sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of Get Smart, the single-camera technique also allowed the series to present fast-paced and tightly edited fight and action sequences reminiscent of the spy dramas that it parodied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For choreographed action or sequences requiring precise editing rhythm, single-camera shooting lets directors craft pacing and coverage deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-camera associated with no laugh track in contemporary sitcoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike single-camera sitcoms from the past, nearly all contemporary comedies shot in this manner are produced without a laugh track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If naturalistic or single-camera comedy tone is desired (no audience laugh cues), single-camera production aligns with that stylistic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blending camera modes for stylistic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Some contemporary shows (e.g., WandaVision; Kevin Can F**k Himself) blend both types of camera usage throughout episodes to achieve different stylistic and narrative effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers can deliberately alternate or mix multi- and single-camera approaches within a series or episode to evoke different eras, contexts, or perspectives; this is a creative option rather than a strict rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for large casts and varied locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-camera was used for shows with large cast, varied locations, and seriocomic tone (example: M*A*S*H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When episodes require location changes, expanded cast blocking, or a tonal blend that benefits from cinematic treatment, single-camera workflows better accommodate those needs despite increased complexity.
